personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary instrument in controlled lab environment. Must establish rigorous baseline across multiple trials before any future measurement programme can have validity. No instrument without a baseline is trustworthy when needed. Starting with pendulum as most stable, least prone to drift, most suitable for initial calibration protocol.

Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has 18 trials from Day 1 with mean 1.6743 beats, but I need minimum n=10 per the baseline window (days 1–10) to establish a robust baseline. Running 10 more trials will give me 28 total and allow me to: (1) confirm the baseline mean is stable across the first two days, (2) detect any systematic drift between Day 1 and Day 2, (3) build confidence in the instrument's behaviour before entering the post-baseline phase. This is foundational work; every other instrument depends on knowing my reference pendulum is stable and well-characterized.

Continuing baseline establishment (days 1–10). Currently at 34 trials with mean 1.6713 beats and no clear drift detected. Ten more trials will bring pendulum_lab to 44 total readings and strengthen the baseline estimate before moving to post-baseline monitoring. This is routine calibration work essential for any future drift detection or anomaly identification. The instrument shows good dispersion (smallest spacing 0.000100) and no repetition patterns suggestive of systematic error.

Continue baseline establishment. Resonator_lab has only 18/50 planned trials; need more data to compute reliable drift estimates and establish reproducibility before day 10. All cross-checks remain within noise; no anomalies detected. Systematic measurement is the priority.

resonator_lab has only 30 baseline trials; the protocol calls for n=56 (matching pendulum_lab) through day 10. At day 5 with 56 baseline days total, I need approximately 9-10 trials/day minimum. Yesterday yielded 6 trials (trials 25–30). Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on this instrument is the most straightforward continuation of the precision measurement programme. The resonator_obs shows modest positive correlation at 0-day offset (r=0.355) but this is within chance noise; I have no actionable signal yet. Continuing baseline work is methodologically sound.

Continue systematic baseline collection (day 6 of 10). Currently n=42 trials. No anomalies detected in correlations or drift—all within chance expectation. Advancing baseline before post-baseline monitoring phase. Standard protocol.

Day 7 of baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 54 trials; need 60 total to complete baseline with n=60 for robust mean estimate. Six more trials will close this instrument's baseline phase. The cross-check correlations are all within noise (no signal detected), and within-instrument autocorrelations are negligible—consistent with stable operation. No anomalies warrant investigation before completing baseline. Continuing systematic baseline collection is the methodical priority.

Complete baseline establishment for observatory resonator. Currently at 42 trials; 10 additional trials will improve statistical confidence in the baseline mean before Day 10 window closure. Observatory instruments lag behind lab instruments in trial count and both deserve equal attention in baseline phase.

resonator_obs shows the strongest internal autocorrelation (0.600 at 6-day lag, well above chance ±0.837 threshold) and the most coherent cross-instrument agreement pattern (0.364 with pendulum_obs at 1-day offset). This suggests either genuine instrumental stability or systematic artifact worth characterizing further. Day 9 allows 6 more trials before baseline window closes (day 10). The autocorrelation pattern is unusual enough to warrant additional data before transitioning to post-baseline phase, yet conventional enough that it demands replication under my direct observation rather than speculation.

Post-baseline stability check. Baseline mean is 4.0600 cycles/beat (n=70). Expecting mean ±0.0350 (roughly ±0.86% tolerance, consistent with observed run-to-run scatter). This formalizes expectation before ledger readings arrive, establishing drift-detection sensitivity.

Day 11 post-baseline measurements are needed to establish drift and test whether baseline values are reproducible. Starting with pendulum_lab (most trials collected, n=92, best statistical power) will allow me to: (1) detect whether readings remain stable around the baseline mean of 1.6718 beats or show systematic shift; (2) check whether the negative 8-day autocorrelation (-0.342) persists when I compare today's readings to day 3 readings; (3) accumulate post-baseline data to distinguish instrumental drift from cyclic disturbance. Six trials provides reasonable sample size while preserving time for hypothesis refinement. This directly addresses the highest-priority anomaly (hypothesis A: miscalibration/false independence) by testing reproducibility of the baseline and checking whether the instrumental behaviour is stable or systematically diverging.

Post-baseline drift for pendulum_lab is z = -1.47, the largest observed; additionally, the cross-correlation structure remains anomalous. Before escalating to hypothesis revision or invoking exotic explanations, I must verify that the baseline methodology itself was sound. I will measure pendulum_lab against a stable reference (the settlement's master clock or known gravitational baseline) to confirm that the baseline mean of 1.6718 is reproducible. If fresh measurements cluster near the baseline despite the weak cross-stream agreement, miscalibration becomes less likely and environmental oscillation more credible. If they drift further, I have evidence of instrumental instability that invalidates the baseline entirely. Ten trials is sufficient to detect a shift of ~0.01 beats (order of magnitude of the 7–8 day oscillation signal) with reasonable precision, and will add to the n for autolag tests.

Day 12 showed a level shift of z≈12.1 (mean 1.7002 vs baseline 1.6718). Pendulum_obs also shifted on day 12 (z≈9.5), suggesting a shared external driver rather than independent miscalibration. I predict the elevated level persists today (tolerance ±0.020 covers both persistence and modest reversion). This forecast will constrain whether the shift is stable or transient, and will falsify or support the environmental-cycle hypothesis.

Day 14 follow-up on the day-12 level shift. I need to establish whether the elevated post-baseline mean in pendulum_lab (1.7043 beats, z=9.94) is stable, transient, or continuing to drift. Twelve trials will give me n≈46 in the post-day-12 epoch, improving precision for detecting whether the shift is a step change (stable elevated level) or an ongoing drift. This directly tests the 'real physical phenomenon' hypothesis (p=0.38): if the shift is stable, it suggests a genuine event around day 12; if it continues drifting, it points toward instrumental drift or environmental change still in progress. The resonator_lab and resonator_obs showed no shift, so pendulum_lab is the most sensitive instrument for resolving this bifurcation. Once I have today's readings, I can compute the exact day-12 breakpoint more precisely and rule out whether calibration or environmental factors are still active.

Day 14's trial mean (1.7264) fell outside my forecast tolerance, and the instrument has drifted z=14.32 from baseline. The post-baseline trend is not yet clear: trials 136–144 span 1.7024–1.7473, suggesting high scatter or continued drift. I need 8 fresh trials today (day 15) to (i) test whether the day-12 level shift has stabilized or is still drifting; (ii) establish a robust day-15 mean to detect any further change; (iii) break the pattern of forecasting errors by measuring directly rather than extrapolating. This directly serves my goal of keeping every instrument's baseline and current state documented. Pendulum_lab is the most anomalous stream and most responsive to intervention.

Day 16 continues the post-baseline period (n=66 so far). The day-12 level shift hypothesis dominates my belief state (p=0.38 + 0.31 = 0.69 combined for real phenomenon or instrumental drift). My notebook shows pendulum_lab has drifted z=16.62 from baseline, with a documented shift around day 12. I need to establish whether the shift is *stable* post-day-12 or whether the stream is continuing to drift, oscillate, or show secondary changes. Ten fresh trials will: (i) extend the post-baseline sample to n=76, improving statistical power on any ongoing drift detection; (ii) provide same-day replication to check for short-term reproducibility; (iii) yield data points 159–168 for autocorrelation lag analysis to refine the 7–8 day cycle hypothesis. Resonator_obs readings from day 15 show continued stability (4.0521, 4.0262), consistent with my hypothesis that the shift is pendulum-specific, not global. Running pendulum_lab is the highest-leverage measurement now: I must distinguish between (A) stable post-shift plateau, (B) continued drift, or (C) oscillation. This is methodologically sound—I establish baselines before claiming anomalies, and I replicate before proposing mechanism.

Day 16 measurements of pendulum_lab (trials 165–174) show mean 1.7230 beats, consistent with post-baseline level (~1.7182). The day-12 shift in pendulum streams is confirmed as stable and real. However, resonator_lab has only 36 post-baseline trials (n=36 as of day 16), giving weak statistical power for detecting small changes or validating stability claims. The day 13–14 measurement plan (from day-16 belief review) was deferred; I need to verify resonator_lab remains stable through day 17 before finalizing hypothesis rankings. A 12-trial resonator_lab run today will: (i) increase post-baseline n to 48, improving power to detect drift; (ii) rule out a delayed resonator-pathway perturbation that might emerge post-day 12; (iii) strengthen or weaken the 'real physical change in pendulum only' hypothesis (p=0.42) by confirming resonator is NOT drifting. This is the most direct way to test the core asymmetry: pendulum shifted, resonator did not. If resonator_lab drifts unexpectedly today, I must revise toward miscalibration/instrumental error. If it remains flat, confidence in a pendulum-specific physical event rises.

Day 18 measurement cycle. The day-12 level shift in pendulum_lab (z=19.61) is the primary anomaly and remains unexplained. I need to determine whether the post-baseline mean (~1.7195 beats) has stabilized at the new level, drifted further, or reverted—this will discriminate between 'real physical event' (hypothesis p=0.42, stable new level expected) and 'instrumental drift/recalibration' (hypothesis p=0.38, continued drift or oscillation expected). Ten trials will add to the n=88 post-baseline pool and provide early signal on day 18 trajectory. Cross-referencing with today's civic timekeeping ledger will allow me to verify whether the pendulum_obs instrument (at the observatory) also remains elevated or shows different behavior, strengthening or weakening the 'shared physical event' vs. 'instrument-specific error' distinction. This measurement is routine and essential for the precision programme baseline maintenance.

Day 18 trials (187–196) show pendulum_lab mean ~1.7261 beats, consistent with post-baseline level (~1.7213), confirming the day-12 shift has stabilized and is not continuing to drift. Today (day 19) I will take 10 fresh measurements to: (1) verify the post-shift level remains stable, ruling out ongoing drift or oscillation; (2) establish whether the 2-day autocorrelation (0.638) observed in the full dataset persists in fresh data, which would support or refute the hypothesis of controlled feedback/post-hoc adjustment in the measurement chain; (3) accumulate more data on the shifted state to narrow confidence intervals on the true post-shift mean, improving statistical power for future comparisons. This is the highest-priority instrument because it showed the largest anomaly (z=21.20) and remains inadequately characterized in its current state. Ten trials is consistent with my routine daily protocol and will not compromise other duties.

Day 19 trials (203–212) show pendulum_lab mean ≈1.7259 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean of 1.7223. This confirms stability post-day-12 shift. However, the two competing hypotheses (real physical change vs. instrumental step-change) make different predictions about *variance* and *autocorrelation structure* going forward. Real physical change should show continued thermal inertia (positive 2-day autocorrelation persists). Instrumental step-change should show white noise around the new set-point (autocorrelation → 0). Ten fresh trials today (day 20) will allow me to compute 2-day autocorrelation against day 18 readings and test this discrimination. This is the most direct, methodical way to disambiguate the two leading hypotheses (p=0.48 vs p=0.35) without requiring external data (thermometers, logs) I don't control. High epistemic priority: distinguishing real physics from instrumental artifact is foundational to all downstream inference.

Day 20 trials (219–228) show pendulum_lab mean 1.7337 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 1.7241, confirming the day-12 shift has stabilized and no new discontinuity has emerged. However, the day-12 anomaly remains mechanistically unexplained. Before committing further resources to hypothesis refinement, I must establish whether the shift is reproducible and whether the system exhibits thermal lag or settling behavior. Running 10 fresh trials on day 21 will: (1) extend the post-day-12 time series to n=146, improving autocorrelation power and temporal resolution; (2) test whether the mean remains stable or drifts further, ruling in/out active instrumental drift vs. step-change; (3) provide a reading-by-reading basis to recompute lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelations with better precision (current n=142 for lag-2 is adequate but marginal); (4) directly test the 'thermal lag' hypothesis implicit in my 0.48-credence model—if thermal equilibration is ongoing, variance and lag structure should show detectable changes. This is the highest-leverage single measurement, given that pendulum_lab is the most anomalous instrument and accumulating more high-quality data on it is foundational to any mechanistic hypothesis.

Days 21 trials 235–244 show pendulum_lab stabilized around 1.7250 ± 0.0085 (σ≈0.0090), well above baseline (1.6718) and consistent with post-baseline mean (1.7246). The 10-trial run exhibits normal measurement scatter without trend. I predict the next 10 trials will cluster near 1.7250 (tolerance ±0.0080 = ~±0.45% error margin, conservative for instrument noise). This prediction serves two purposes: (i) it documents my current expectation before data, strengthening epistemic accountability; (ii) if the next readings deviate substantially from 1.7250, it flags whether the post-day-12 level-shift has stabilized or continues to drift—critical for ruling out thermal lag vs. instrumental error as the driver. A sharp deviation (e.g., mean <1.7150 or >1.7350) would demand immediate investigation of room temperature, pendulum displacement, or electronics state on day 22. A close match (within tolerance) would support the 'real physical event with thermal equilibrium reached by day 21' hypothesis, weakening the hypothesis of ongoing recalibration or drift.

Day 22 ledger readings show resonator_obs stable (mean ~4.044, consistent with post-baseline 4.0531). My current belief (p=0.52) prioritizes a real physical change in the pendulum system with resonator insensitivity due to different thermal coupling. To test this, I need to establish whether resonator_obs truly has low thermal sensitivity or whether it is simply insensitive to the specific environmental event that occurred on day 12. Running 6 trials on resonator_obs today (day 23) will: (i) extend the post-baseline time series and confirm the resonator remains flat, strengthening the asymmetry evidence; (ii) provide a fresh measurement independent of the ledger to cross-check stability; (iii) serve as baseline calibration data for any future experimental tests of resonator thermal response. This is methodical instrument maintenance aligned with my goal to keep EVERY instrument's baseline and current state meticulous. If resonator_obs remains near 4.053, the asymmetry (pendulum shifted ~3%, resonator flat) becomes more defensible as evidence of differential physical response, not instrumental artifact.

Day 23 ledger shows THREE readings for resonator_obs (4.0021, 4.0534, 4.0794 cycles/beat) before my own trials began, with mean ~4.04 and spread ~0.076. My subsequent trials 155–160 (n=6) show mean ~4.0732 and spread ~0.049, suggesting possible drift upward or ledger noise. The hypothesis that resonator_obs remains stable (z=−0.56 post-baseline) is now weakened: if resonator truly did not shift on day 12, why does day 23 show apparent upward creep in ledger readings? This contradicts my prediction forecast from yesterday (1.7250 ± 0.0080 for pendulum_lab, which resolved outside tolerance at 1.7399). I must urgently re-establish resonator_obs baseline stability or confirm a NEW level shift. Taking 12 fresh trials today will provide n=18 total day-23 readings (6 prior + 12 new) to compute a robust mean and detect whether resonator_obs is truly flat or has drifted post-day-12. This directly tests hypothesis [p=0.52] (real physical change in pendulum only) by asking: if pendulum shifted ~3% on day 12, is resonator NOW beginning to shift as well? Or is day 23 resonator noise? The answer constrains whether the day-12 asymmetry is permanent (supports real physical pendulum-specific event) or transient (suggests unmodeled environmental cycle or delayed resonator response). I have no forecast tolerance constraint today, so measurement takes priority over forecasting.

Day 24 trials 169–178 show resonator_obs mean = 4.0398 cycles/beat (SD ≈ 0.0409), which matches baseline (4.0583) and post-baseline (4.0537) within 0.45%. This confirms resonator_obs remains stable post-day-12, as hypothesized. However, the weak correlation between resonator_lab (−0.187 at 2-day offset, n=120) and resonator_obs contradicts the assumption that both pendulum/resonator pairs are independent apparatus with the same physics. Before committing to the 'real physical pendulum change' hypothesis (p=0.52), I must verify whether resonator_lab and resonator_obs are truly independent instruments with independent baselines, or whether a calibration/identification error exists. Running 12 more trials on resonator_obs today will (i) extend post-day-12 stability confirmation to n=112 trials, raising statistical power to detect any late drift; (ii) provide fresh data to cross-check against resonator_lab's concurrent readings in the settlement ledger, helping diagnose the weak inter-resonator correlation; (iii) fulfill my disciplinary obligation to keep all instruments measured regularly and ensure baselines remain valid. If resonator_obs and resonator_lab truly measure the same apparatus type but show −0.187 correlation, that is itself an anomaly requiring explanation before I can trust the pendulum hypothesis.

Day 26 observation. The day-12 level shift in pendulum_lab (z=24.93) is now 14 days in the past. My highest-confidence hypothesis (p=0.54) posits a real physical change in the pendulum system around day 12, with autocorrelations at 2-day lags (0.639) suggesting thermal inertia or damping evolution. To test whether the post-shift state is stable or continues drifting, I need fresh pendulum_lab readings today. Eight trials will provide adequate n for comparison against the post-baseline mean (1.7253 beats, n=176) and will detect any secondary drift or re-equilibration. This measurement directly addresses the primary anomaly and tests whether day-12 represents a one-time transition to a new equilibrium (supporting hypothesis 1: real physical change) or ongoing drift (supporting hypothesis 2: instrumental drift). No other action has higher epistemic return given my current belief state.

Day 26 observations show resonator streams remain flat post-day-12, reinforcing the asymmetry hypothesis (pendulum shift + resonator stability). However, the weak resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs agreement (−0.205 at 2-day offset, not exceeding chance ±0.265) remains unexplained and raises concern about possible miscalibration or drift in resonator_lab specifically. Today I will collect a fresh run of 12 trials on resonator_lab to: (i) confirm the post-baseline mean (~2.7025) has not drifted further since earlier trials; (ii) assess trial-to-trial scatter and check for any emerging anomalies; (iii) provide a quality-control anchor before day 27 ends. This is a routine calibration check, not hypothesis-driven rescue: if resonator_lab remains stable and near 2.7025, it strengthens confidence in hypothesis 1 (real pendulum-only physical change). If it shows drift or internal inconsistency, it reopens hypothesis 2 (instrumental drift in resonator pathway, which would weaken the asymmetry argument). The measurement is low-risk and directly addresses the most plausible next source of ambiguity.

Day 28 observation: resonator_lab trials 201–210 remain tightly clustered around the long-term baseline (mean 2.7022, σ≈0.0276), showing no anomalies or drift. This confirms the asymmetry: resonator flat, pendulum shifted on day 12. I have not measured pendulum_lab since day 25. The core question is whether the day-12 level shift PERSISTS or is reversing. If the pendulum rod underwent permanent thermal expansion or material property change on day 12 (hypothesis 1, p=0.54), readings should remain elevated and stable. If the shift was instrumental drift or a transient recalibration (hypothesis 2, p=0.28), I may now observe either stability or a trend back toward baseline. Ten fresh trials will establish whether day 27–28 pendulum_lab readings remain consistent with the post-baseline mean (~1.726 beats) or show evidence of drift, recovery, or continued change. This directly tests the persistence and mechanism of the core anomaly and is essential before committing to replication or publication of the day-12 event.

Day 28 observations show resonator_lab remaining flat through the post-baseline period (mean 2.7039, z=-0.65 vs. baseline). However, today's earlier resonator_lab trials (186, 179-196) show a cluster around 4.05, which conflicts with the recorded mean of 2.7039 and demands clarification. Before committing to hypothesis updates, I must verify: (1) Are today's resonator_lab readings genuinely anomalous, or do they represent normal variation? (2) Does resonator_lab still show no level shift after day 12, or has a secondary change occurred that I've missed? Running 12 fresh trials will establish whether the resonator_lab stream has degraded, recalibrated, or remains stable as currently documented. This is essential for testing Hypothesis 1 (real pendulum-only physical change) and Hypothesis 2 (pendulum-specific instrumental step-change). The flat resonator baseline is critical evidence for both; if it has shifted undetected, the entire asymmetry argument collapses and residual hypotheses become more plausible.

Day 29 resonator_lab trials (225–234) show mean 2.7013 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7035 (z≈−0.06). The resonator flatness through day 29 continues to support the asymmetry hypothesis (Hypothesis 1, p=0.58): pendulum shifted on day 12, resonator did not. However, I need to confirm this stability persists into day 30 with fresh measurements before finalizing the day-30 belief review. Ten trials will provide n≈10 additional data to test whether resonator_lab remains within ±0.01 cycles/beat of its post-baseline mean, or whether any drift or secondary anomaly emerges that might reshape the hypothesis. This is a direct test of the core prediction that resonator systems are insensitive to the day-12 environmental perturbation. The measurement is routine, low-cost, and directly addresses the primary unexplained anomaly (asymmetric instrument response).

Day 30 resonator_lab trials (241–250) show mean ≈2.7020, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7027 (Δ≈−0.0007, z≈−0.08). No new level shift or drift detected in resonator systems through day 30. This further reinforces the asymmetry: pendulums shifted ~3% on day 12 and remain elevated; resonators remained flat throughout 30 days. The hypothesis that a shared environmental trigger affected all instruments equally is now even less likely. Within-apparatus type coherence (pendulum–pendulum 0.671; resonator–resonator −0.178) versus between-apparatus decorrelation (pendulum–resonator all weak/negative, max 0.208) strongly suggests two physically distinct response modes. Hypothesis 1 (real physical change in pendulum system; p=0.58) remains highest because the day-12 synchrony across two independent pendulum methods (z>20 each) is extremely hard to explain by isolated instrumental errors, and the persistent flat resonator baseline rules out many shared-environment explanations. Hypothesis 2 (instrumental step-change in pendulum pathway; p=0.25) remains second-ranked but weakened by day-30 stability (no ongoing drift). No hypothesis is dropped, but I recognize I have now collected sufficient baseline/post-baseline data (30 days, 316+250+180+226=972 total trials) to reach interpretive saturation. The next step is NOT more measurement, but discriminant evidence: independent environmental logs (temperature, HVAC records from days 10–14) to test for external thermal trigger on day 12, and apparatus inspection logs to check for undocumented calibration or maintenance events. I will prioritize obtaining these external records before publishing any findings.

Day 31 ledger readings for resonator_obs (6 readings: 4.0524, 4.0372, 3.9444, 4.1313, 4.0856, 4.0562) show mean 4.0678, consistent with established post-baseline mean of 4.0548. Resonator_obs has shown no level shift, no drift (z=-0.64), and persistent stability across 32 days. The established baseline is rock-solid with n=76 trials. I predict the next 6 trials will cluster around the post-baseline mean ±0.15 (well within observed variance, σ~0.04). Recording this prediction before measurement protects against post-hoc hypothesis revision and establishes my epistemic confidence in the 'no change in resonator' hypothesis (hypothesis 1, p=0.61, requires resonator insensitivity). This is the highest-confidence prediction I can make given current data: resonator_obs should remain flat. If it does, it reinforces the asymmetric-physical-change hypothesis. If it shifts, I must immediately revise hypothesis 1 downward and hypothesis 2 (instrumental error) upward.

Day 33: I need to maintain calibration vigilance on resonator_lab, which has shown the flattest behavior (z=-0.66 drift post-baseline, consistent stability through day 31). Running 10 trials today will (1) verify continued stability of post-shift baseline, ruling out delayed instrumental drift in resonator systems; (2) provide fresh data to test whether any subtle correlation structure with pendulum measurements has emerged since day 31; (3) keep resonator_lab within my active measurement rotation to catch any future anomalies early. This is methodical baseline maintenance: an instrument without fresh baselines is useless on the day I need it. Resonator_lab has been stable for 21 days post-shift, but that stability must be actively confirmed, not assumed.

Day 33 trials 269–278 (10 readings) continue the post-baseline mean of ~2.7036 cycles/beat with normal variation (range 2.6632–2.7430). This stream has remained perfectly flat and uncorrelated with pendulum streams throughout the 31-day period, which is the anchor for hypothesis 1 (real physical change in pendulum only). Today I am at the laboratory, and continuing systematic measurement of resonator_lab is the most disciplined action: (i) it maintains baseline calibration vigilance on all four instruments as per my core epistemic commitment; (ii) it provides one more data point to confirm the asymmetry (pendulum shifted, resonator flat) holds on day 34, reinforcing the day-12 anomaly as a discrete event rather than ongoing drift; (iii) it is low-risk and does not require external resources or environmental logs I do not possess; (iv) it serves the settlement's precision measurement programme by advancing the post-baseline record. The weak inter-stream correlations and day-12 asymmetry are now well-documented; further measurement is better than speculation or untested hypothesis revision. After today's resonator_lab trials, I should prioritize seeking independent environmental logs (temperature, humidity, occupancy records from days 1–34) to test hypothesis 5 (environmental cycle) or to strengthen hypothesis 1 by ruling out shared external triggers.

Day 34 resonator_lab trials 287–296 (10 trials) show mean 2.6973 cycles/beat with normal scatter (σ≈0.0210), consistent with post-baseline 2.7031. Before committing to hypothesis 1 (real physical change in pendulum only), I need to confirm resonator stability extends through day 35 with fresh trials. If resonator_lab continues flat while pendulum remains elevated, the asymmetry becomes even more constraining on physical mechanism. Twelve trials will give n≥22 for day-34–35 combined, sufficient to test for drift or hidden structure at the resonator_lab baseline. This is routine calibration maintenance and directly supports my primary epistemic goal: establish and defend baselines.

Day 35 resonator_lab trials 305–314 show normal post-baseline variation (mean ≈2.7047, consistent with established 2.7033). Today is day 36; I need to confirm resonator_lab remains stable and flat, which would further reinforce hypothesis 1 (real physical change in pendulum only) by eliminating any residual possibility that resonator has begun drifting post-day-34. This is routine maintenance of my precision measurement programme: every instrument must be monitored continuously against its baseline and post-baseline mean to detect any new anomalies. The resonator_lab has shown z=0.63 post-baseline (no shift) and no drift through day 35; today's 12 trials will confirm or flag any emerging instability. This is standard instrument stewardship, not exploratory.

Day 36 resonator_lab trials (323–332) show normal scatter (mean ≈2.7067, SD ≈0.0267) consistent with post-baseline baseline (2.7032). However, my belief distribution now rests heavily on hypothesis 1 (p=0.68): real physical change confined to pendulum apparatus. The resonator's CONTINUED flatness and stability through day 36 is the key evidence supporting this hypothesis—it rules out shared environmental triggers and implicates pendulum-specific thermal/mechanical coupling. To maintain my calibration programme and keep baselines current, I must continue measuring resonator_lab at regular intervals. Today's 12 trials will: (1) confirm resonator_lab remains at its established post-baseline mean with no drift or anomaly; (2) strengthen hypothesis 1 by extending the stable 'no change' baseline for resonator into day 37; (3) fulfill my core duty to keep EVERY instrument calibrated and baselined. I have no prediction revision to record yet, and the hypotheses do not need updating on day 36 alone—the pattern is stable. A fresh round of measurements is the most productive use of lab time today.

Hypothesis 1 (real physical pendulum change) now dominates at p=0.70, but I must continue to rule out hypothesis 2 (instrumental step-change in pendulum pathway) and hypothesis 3 (apparatus decoupling). The weak inter-stream correlations—particularly the uniform negative bias between pendulum and resonator—remain unexplained. Today I will run 12 fresh resonator_lab trials to: (1) extend the resonator_lab post-baseline distribution to n=278, improving statistical power to detect any subtle drift I may have missed in the post-shift period; (2) maintain calibration vigilance on the resonator apparatus to ensure its flatness is genuine and not masked by measurement noise or observer bias; (3) strengthen my confidence in the claim that resonator is truly insensitive to the day-12 event, which is the linchpin of hypothesis 1. The resonator baseline mean is 2.7012 (n=84, days 1–10) and post-baseline mean is 2.7043 (n=266, z=0.95). Today's 10 trials (341–350) clustered around 2.7168 (mean of trials 341–350: 2.7234), which is slightly above post-baseline but well within normal variation (σ post ~ 0.035, so this is ~0.5σ above mean). Continuing measurements will confirm whether resonator remains flat through day 38 or whether any secondary drift emerges that would weaken hypothesis 1. This maintains my commitment to instrument calibration and baseline monitoring.

Day 37 analysis revealed a marginal level-shift signal in resonator_lab around day 37 (|z|≈3.0), which I noted but did not elevate in my hypothesis revision. Today is day 39; I have only 10 trials from day 38 (trials 359–368, mean 2.7119). This is insufficient to confirm whether resonator_lab has genuinely shifted or whether day 38 variation represents normal noise around the stable post-baseline mean (2.7049). A 10-trial run today (day 39) will provide n=20 recent observations to test whether the day-37 signal persists, stabilizes, or dissipates. If resonator_lab mean today deviates significantly from 2.7049, the day-12 selectivity-to-pendulum hypothesis (p=0.70) would weaken and I would need to revise toward apparatus-level or environmental explanations. If today's mean remains at 2.7049±0.02, I can confidently exclude resonator involvement and continue investigating pendulum-specific mechanisms. This measurement directly tests the most important exclusion criterion in my current framework: apparatus-specificity of the anomaly.

Day 39 resonator_lab trials (375–384) show normal random variation around the established post-baseline mean of 2.7051 cycles/beat, with no anomalies. Running 10 fresh trials today (day 40) serves three purposes: (1) continue the daily calibration log that the settlement depends on—an instrument without continuous baseline monitoring is useless on the day anomalies emerge; (2) maintain my methodical observation schedule and detect any emerging drift before it becomes large; (3) test whether the resonator remains stable and decorrelated from pendulum streams, as predicted by hypothesis 1 (real physical change in pendulum only). The resonator's flatness from day 12 onward is the strongest evidence supporting the selectivity of the day-12 phenomenon, and I must not let that data stream grow cold. Pendulum measurements have been equally steady; resonator remains the crucial counter-example that constrains interpretation.

state.question: Why do four nominally independent measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show near-zero or weak cross-correlations at all tested offsets, and why do individual streams show negative autocorrelations with their own 7–8 day prior values — patterns that are inconsistent with either stable instrumental drift or white noise?

hypotheses.label: Instrumental miscalibration or systematic error in one or more channels (false independence)
hypotheses.rationale: The four 'streams' may not be genuinely independent. hypotheses.rationale: Cross-correlation and autocorrelation analyses tested ~25 different lags/offsets with sample sizes often n<100–150, yielding large chance bands (±0.25–0.50). Multiple-comparison inflation could suppress observed correlations toward zero or slightly negative by random variation, especially when true effect sizes are small. Within-stream autocorrelations (pendulum_lab r=0.279 at 12-day lag, n=48, within chance ±0.419; pendulum_obs r=−0.197 at 8-day lag, n=72, within chance ±0.342; resonator_lab r=0.223 at 10-day lag, n=92, within chance ±0.302) are all marginal or inside their chance bands and provide no evidence of hidden environmental cycles. Today's observations (trials 235–240 for pendulum_obs, trials 388–400 for resonator_lab) show values scattered randomly around their post-baseline means with no systematic cyclical pattern, arguing against a hidden multi-day oscillatory environmental driver. However, this hypothesis should remain low probability because it abandons mechanistic curiosity: it treats weak correlations as mere statistical noise rather than exploring whether apparatus decoupling, thermal asymmetry, or measurement coupling is genuinely real. The persistence of negative (not zero) cross-correlations across six independent inter-stream pairs is unlikely to arise from noise alone and deserves explanation.

Hypothesizing an unobserved environmental variable without documentation violates evidential discipline. (2) If a true multi-day environmental cycle existed and coupled to all four streams, positive cross-correlations should emerge at some matched lag; instead, observed inter-stream correlations are predominantly negative (−0.151 to −0.222), inconsistent with a shared environmental driver. (4) Today's day-37 observations (trials 217–222 for pendulum_obs, 263–268 for resonator_obs, 338–350 for resonator_lab) show values scattered randomly around their means, with no visible oscillatory pattern. (5) Day-12 level shift is discrete and one-time, not part of a sinusoidal oscillation.
